newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks close lower on consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks close lower on consolidation.

text.p: Seoul stocks closed lower on Monday as the market continued its consolidation and brokers said late selling of some blue chips by onshore funds reversed early technical rebound.
Brokers said investors shrugged off a rally in high-tech stocks in Tokyo.
"With no fresh impetus to affect the market, many investors stayed on the sidelines," said Woo Sang-chul at Tongyang Securities. "The market will be lethargic until August."
The composite stock index shed 2.82 points to 764.45, off the day's high of 770.73.
Brokers said blue chips were mixed.
POSCO and SK Telecom fell on sales by onshore funds. The steelmaker lost 1,600 won to 61,200 and the mobile telephone service provider shed 8,000 won to 475,000.
But LG Information and Communication rose 1,500 won to 111,500 and Samsung Electronics closed unchanged at 67,600, off a day low of 66,600.

Some nervous investors renewed their concerns about financial problems in smaller business conglomerates on the news Hyundai Group was considering raising two trillion won by selling assets in the second half.
The group was also studying a plan to generate another one trillion won by offering rights issues in its affiliates.
"The news reflected worsening financial status among Korean business groups," said Park Jong-kwon at Coryo Securities.
Buying interest remained strong in some smaller companies in the belief of improved first-half earnings.

Halla Engineering and Construction went limit up, gaining 1,700 won to 24,000 with heavy volume of 480,630 shares. Brass-bar producer Daewoo Metal closed at its 1997 high of 16,500 won, up 1,200 with hefty volume of 547,840 shares changing hands.
Brokers said margin loans exceeding customers deposits at brokerage houses also pressured investors sentiment.

The court-appointed management of Hanbo Steel said the recurring loss in the failed Hanbo Steel declined to 84.1 billion won in the first half of calendar 1997 from a 91.8 billion loss a year earlier. But investors ignored the news and Hanbo Steel shed 90 won to 4,600.
Brokers said investors would not show any interest in Hanbo, until a third party bought the troubled steelmaker.
Woo at Tonyang Securities said investors would take a wait-and-see attitude until interim corporate results were reported.
South Korea's listed companies planned to release their six-month business performance results in mid-August.
But Casey Choe at Union Bank of Switzlerland said the market would rally, if investors saw any positive signs about interest rates, the yen's strength and macro-economic indicators.
